label: Lesson 1
title: The nature of electromagnetic radiation
summary: Electromagnetic radiation is a wave and a stream of particles at the same time. This lesson sets out both pictures: the oscillating electric and magnetic fields of the wave, the photons of the quantum view, and the relationships that connect wavelength, frequency and energy across the electromagnetic spectrum.

intro.text: Spectroscopy is the study of how matter interacts with electromagnetic radiation. Before any of it makes sense you need a clear picture of what that radiation is. This lesson gives two pictures that are both true, and shows how they fit together.

The first is the *wave* picture: light is an oscillating electromagnetic field that travels through space. The second is the *quantum* picture: light arrives in discrete packets of energy called photons. Neither alone explains everything you will see in a spectrum.

intro.title: The two pictures in one sentence
intro.body: Electromagnetic radiation is a transverse electromagnetic wave whose energy is delivered in discrete photons, so its wavelength, frequency and photon energy are linked by c = \u03bbf and E = hf.

sections.title: The wave nature of EMR
sections.summary: Electromagnetic radiation is a transverse wave: an electric field and a magnetic field oscillating together and travelling through space.
keyPoints: EMR is a transverse wave made of an oscillating electric field E and magnetic field B.
The two fields are mutually perpendicular and both are perpendicular to the direction of travel.
The wavelength λ is the distance between corresponding points on the wave; the frequency f is the number of cycles per second.
In a vacuum every form of EMR travels at the same speed, the speed of light c, with c = λf.

blocks.text: Start with the wave picture. Electromagnetic radiation is a *transverse wave*: a disturbance that travels forward while the things doing the oscillating move at right angles to the direction of travel. What oscillates is not a material but a pair of fields.

The first is the *electric field* E, the second the *magnetic field* B. They rise and fall together as a sine wave, and they are oriented at right angles to each other and to the direction in which the wave moves. A wave is drawn as two sine curves threaded along a common axis, one for E and one for B.

blocks.alt: An electromagnetic wave, with the electric field E oscillating vertically and the magnetic field B oscillating from side to side at right angles, both perpendicular to the direction of travel, which is marked by an arrow labelled at the speed of light c.
blocks.caption: An electromagnetic wave. The electric field **E** (red) and the magnetic field **B** (blue) oscillate at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, and the whole pattern moves forward at the speed of light **c**.

blocks.text: Two lengths describe the wave. The *wavelength* λ is the distance from one crest to the next, or between any two corresponding points. The *amplitude* is the height of the wave, which sets how strong the fields are, and with the intensity of the light. The *frequency* f is how many complete cycles pass a fixed point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).

blocks.caption: The speed of light links wavelength and frequency

blocks.text: In a vacuum all electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed, the speed of light c, about 3.0 × 10^8 m/s. Because that speed is fixed, wavelength and frequency are locked together: a longer wavelength must mean a lower frequency, and a shorter wavelength a higher one.

blocks.title: One wave, many names
blocks.body: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all the same kind of wave. Only their wavelength and frequency differ, and that single difference changes everything about how they interact with matter.

sections.title: The quantum nature of EMR
sections.summary: Light also behaves as a stream of discrete energy packets called photons, each carrying an energy set by its frequency.
keyPoints: EMR is absorbed and emitted in discrete packets of energy called photons or quanta.
The energy of one photon is E = hf, where h is the Planck constant.
Photon energy is proportional to frequency: higher frequency means higher energy.
A high-frequency photon, such as an X-ray photon, carries far more energy than a low-frequency radio photon.

blocks.text: The wave picture cannot explain everything. When light is absorbed or emitted, matter does not take it in continuously: it exchanges energy in fixed, discrete amounts called *quanta*. The smallest packet of electromagnetic energy is the *photon*.
A photon is not a tiny ball with a definite position. It is a packet of energy whose size is fixed by the frequency of the radiation. The higher the frequency, the more energy each photon carries.

blocks.caption: Energy of a single photon, with h the Planck constant

blocks.text: Here h is the *Planck constant*, about 6.626 × 10^-34 J s. It is a very small number, which is why a beam of ordinary light, carrying enormous numbers of photons, looks perfectly continuous. The quantisation is only visible when energy is exchanged one photon at a time.

blocks.title: The same relation, two symbols
blocks.body: You will see frequency written as both f and the Greek letter nu (ν). E = hf and E = hν mean exactly the same thing: photon energy equals the Planck constant times the frequency.

blocks.text: Because photon energy rises with frequency, an X-ray photon carries far more energy than a photon of visible light, and a radio photon carries far less still. This single fact underlies why X-rays can ionise atoms while radio waves pass through a body almost untouched.

sections.title: Key properties of EMR
sections.summary: Four properties describe how electromagnetic radiation behaves: it propagates at c, needs no medium, forms a continuous spectrum, and interacts with matter as waves and as particles.
keyPoints: EMR propagates through space at the speed of light c.
It requires no medium: it travels through a vacuum, unlike sound.
It forms a continuous electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to gamma rays.
It interacts with matter as waves (diffraction, interference) and as particles (absorption, emission, the photoelectric effect).

blocks.text: Four properties summarise how electromagnetic radiation behaves, and each one matters for spectroscopy.

items: *Propagation*: it travels through space at the speed of light c.
*No medium needed*: it can travel through a vacuum, because it is a disturbance of fields rather than of matter.
*Continuous spectrum*: every wavelength belongs to one single, unbroken spectrum.
*Dual interaction*: it meets matter as waves in some experiments and as particles in others.

blocks.title: Propagation
blocks.body: **Propagation** is the travel of a wave through space. The electric and magnetic fields oscillate in place, and the pattern they form moves forward, carrying energy from the source to the detector. In a vacuum every electromagnetic wave propagates at the same speed, **c**, which is why wavelength and frequency stay locked together.

blocks.text: The absence of a medium is worth pausing on. Sound is a vibration of a material and must have something to travel through; that is why a ringing bell in an evacuated jar is silent. Light needs no such thing, because the electric and magnetic fields carry it directly. Light crosses the vacuum of space from the Sun to reach us.

blocks.title: Where the dual behaviour shows up
blocks.body: Wave behaviour is seen in *diffraction* and *interference*; particle behaviour is seen in *absorption*, *emission* and the *photoelectric effect*. You will meet each one later in this course, and both faces are needed to explain a real spectrum.

sections.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
sections.summary: The spectrum runs from long-wavelength radio waves to short-wavelength gamma rays; shorter wavelength means higher frequency and higher photon energy.
keyPoints: The spectrum is continuous, but it is divided into named regions for convenience.
Wavelength decreases and energy increases as you move from radio waves towards gamma rays.
Each region matches particular kinds of transition: nuclear, electronic, vibrational or rotational.
A photon of energy E = hc/λ can only drive a transition whose energy gap it matches.

blocks.text: Ordered by wavelength, the electromagnetic spectrum divides into named regions. The names are convenient labels on a continuous range, not sharp boundaries. As wavelength falls, both frequency and photon energy rise.

blocks.alt: The electromagnetic spectrum drawn as one continuous bar, from gamma rays and X-rays at the short-wavelength, high-energy end through ultraviolet, visible, infrared and microwaves to radio waves at the long-wavelength, low-energy end.
blocks.caption: The electromagnetic spectrum. The regions are named parts of one continuous range: as wavelength falls from radio waves towards gamma rays, frequency and photon energy rise.

blocks.text: The right-hand column is the heart of spectroscopy. A molecule absorbs a photon only when its energy matches a gap between two of the molecule’s own energy levels. Large gaps, such as those between electronic states, need high-energy ultraviolet or visible photons; the small gaps of molecular vibration and rotation need infrared and microwave photons.

blocks.caption: Photon energy in terms of wavelength

blocks.text: Because c is fixed, the energy of a photon can be written just as well in terms of its wavelength. This is the form used most often in spectroscopy, since instruments measure wavelength far more naturally than frequency.

sections.title: Relationships between the parameters
sections.summary: The three central relationships link speed, wavelength, frequency and energy, and let any one of them be found from another.
keyPoints: Wavelength, frequency and the speed of light are linked by c = λf.
Photon energy, frequency and wavelength are linked by E = hf = hc/λ.
Multiply frequency by wavelength to get c; divide c by wavelength to get frequency.
Energy rises as wavelength falls, which is why short-wave radiation is the energetic end of the spectrum.

blocks.text: Everything in this lesson follows from two short equations. The first connects the wave parameters; the second adds the photon energy.

blocks.alt: A graph of photon energy E against frequency f: a straight line through the origin with the points f and 2f marked, showing that doubling the frequency doubles the energy and that the slope is the Planck constant.
blocks.caption: Photon energy rises in step with frequency. The graph is a straight line through the origin whose slope is the Planck constant **h**, so doubling the frequency doubles the photon energy.

blocks.text: Rearranged, they let you move between any pair of quantities. If you know a wavelength, dividing the speed of light by it gives the frequency. Multiply that frequency by h and you have the photon energy. Since all four numbers are tied together, spectroscopy is largely the business of measuring one and inferring the rest.

blocks.title: The energy of a green photon
blocks.given: Green light has a wavelength of 550 nm. Find its frequency and the energy of one photon. Take c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s and h = 6.626 × 10^-34 J s.
steps: Convert the wavelength to metres: λ = 550 nm = 550 × 10^-9 m = 5.50 × 10^-7 m.
blocks.result: The photon has a frequency of about 5.5 × 10^14 Hz and carries about 3.6 × 10^-19 J of energy.

blocks.title: The single thread through the spectrum
blocks.body: Every region of the spectrum obeys the same two equations. What distinguishes an X-ray from a radio wave is simply where it sits on the scale of λ, f and E, and that position decides which transitions it can drive.

cta.title: Check what you have learned
cta.body: Take the Lesson 1 quiz to test the wave and quantum pictures, the spectrum, and the relationships between the parameters.

questions.question: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric field and the magnetic field are:
options: Parallel to each other and to the direction of travel
Mutually perpendicular and both perpendicular to the direction of travel
Both parallel to the direction of travel
Parallel to each other but perpendicular to the direction of travel
questions.explanation: The electric and magnetic fields oscillate at right angles to each other and to the direction in which the wave moves, which is what makes the wave transverse.

questions.question: In a vacuum, all electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed.
questions.explanation: Every region of the spectrum travels at c in a vacuum. What differs between radio waves and gamma rays is the wavelength and frequency, not the speed.

questions.question: Infrared radiation has a wavelength of 1.0 × 10^-6 m. What is its frequency, in hertz? Take c = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s.
The wavelength of a wave is the distance between:
options: The origin and the first crest
Two corresponding points on the wave, such as crest to crest
One crest and the nearest trough
The start and end of the wave
questions.explanation: The wavelength is the repeat distance of the wave: from one crest to the next, or equivalently between any two corresponding points.

questions.question: The energy carried by a single photon is given by:
questions.explanation: A photon’s energy is the Planck constant times the frequency, E = hf. Higher frequency therefore means more energetic photons.

questions.question: A photon of ultraviolet light carries more energy than a photon of visible light.
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet has a higher frequency than visible light, and since E = hf, a higher frequency means a more energetic photon.

questions.question: The quantum picture of light is needed to explain:
options: The absorption and emission of light in discrete packets
The bending of light at a glass surface
questions.explanation: Absorption and emission happen one photon at a time, so they require the quantum picture. Diffraction and interference are explained by the wave picture.

questions.question: A photon has a frequency of 1.0 × 10^15 Hz. What is its energy, in joules? Take h = 6.626 × 10^-34 J s.
Which statement about electromagnetic radiation is correct?
options: It can travel only through a material medium
It cannot travel through a vacuum
It travels through a vacuum without needing a medium
It travels more slowly than sound in a vacuum
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic radiation needs no medium: the oscillating fields carry it through empty space. Sound, by contrast, does need a medium.

questions.question: Which observations are evidence for the wave nature of light? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Diffraction, interference and polarisation are all wave phenomena. The photoelectric effect is evidence for the particle nature.

questions.question: Which are true of electromagnetic radiation? Select all that apply.
options: It propagates at the speed of light in vacuum
It requires a medium to travel
It interacts with matter as both waves and particles
questions.explanation: EMR forms a continuous spectrum, travels at c in vacuum, and shows both wave and particle behaviour. It does not require a medium.

questions.question: Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum has the highest photon energy?
questions.explanation: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths and therefore the highest frequencies and the highest photon energies, at the far end of the spectrum.

questions.question: As you move from radio waves towards gamma rays across the spectrum:
options: Both wavelength and energy stay constant
questions.explanation: Moving towards gamma rays the wavelength falls while frequency and photon energy rise. The two trends run in opposite directions.

questions.question: A photon has a wavelength of 500 nm. What is its energy, in joules? Take h = 6.626 × 10^-34 J s and c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s.
Vibrational transitions in molecules are typically probed with which radiation?
questions.explanation: The energy gaps of molecular vibration match infrared photons. Electronic transitions need visible or ultraviolet, and nuclear transitions need gamma rays.

questions.question: The relationship between wavelength λ, frequency f and the speed of light c is:
questions.explanation: The speed of a wave equals its wavelength times its frequency, c = λf. This fixed product is why longer wavelength means lower frequency.

questions.question: Visible light has a wavelength of 600 nm. What is its frequency, in hertz? Take c = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s.
Shorter wavelength radiation carries more energy per photon than longer wavelength radiation.
questions.explanation: Since E = hc/λ, energy is inversely proportional to wavelength: the shorter the wavelength, the greater the photon energy.

questions.question: Which equations correctly relate the parameters of electromagnetic radiation? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: c = λf, E = hf and E = hc/λ are all correct. The relation λ = Ec is not; it confuses the roles of wavelength and energy.

questions.question: The amplitude of an electromagnetic wave tells you about:
options: the strength of its oscillating fields
how many cycles pass each second
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the height of the wave. It sets how strong the electric and magnetic fields are, and therefore how bright or intense the light is. Wavelength and frequency are separate properties.

questions.question: Why does a beam of ordinary light look perfectly smooth rather than grainy, even though it is made of photons?
options: photons are too heavy to see
each photon carries a tiny energy and enormous numbers of them arrive every second
light contains no photons until it hits something
all the photons merge into one long wave
questions.explanation: The Planck constant is tiny, so a single photon carries very little energy. An everyday beam carries so many photons per second that the arrivals blend into a smooth, continuous stream.

questions.question: Electromagnetic radiation must have a medium to travel through.
questions.explanation: It needs no medium at all: the oscillating fields carry it through a vacuum. Sound, by contrast, is a vibration of matter and does need a medium, which is why a bell in an evacuated jar cannot be heard.

questions.question: Infrared radiation has a wavelength of 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. What is its frequency, in hertz? Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
If you double the frequency of some radiation, what happens to its photon energy and its wavelength?
options: the energy doubles and the wavelength halves
the energy halves and the wavelength doubles
both the energy and the wavelength double
both the energy and the wavelength stay the same
questions.explanation: Energy is E = hf, so doubling f doubles the energy. Wavelength is λ = c/f, so doubling f halves the wavelength. The two move in opposite directions.

questions.question: Compare radio waves with ultraviolet light. Which of these are greater for the ultraviolet? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet has a higher frequency and therefore a higher photon energy than radio waves. Its wavelength is shorter, not longer, and the speed in a vacuum is c for every kind of radiation.

questions.question: The amplitude of a light wave chiefly determines its:
questions.explanation: A larger amplitude means stronger fields and hence a more intense beam. Wavelength, frequency and speed are set by the source and the medium, not by the amplitude.

questions.question: The wavelength of a wave is the distance between:
options: a crest and the adjacent trough
questions.explanation: Wavelength is the distance over which the pattern repeats, for example crest to crest or trough to trough.

questions.question: Frequency is measured in:
questions.explanation: Frequency is the number of cycles per second, and one cycle per second is one hertz (Hz).

questions.question: For light in a vacuum, if the wavelength is doubled the frequency:
questions.explanation: In a vacuum c = λf is fixed, so λ and f are inversely proportional. Doubling λ halves f.

questions.question: In a vacuum, all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed.
questions.explanation: Every form of electromagnetic radiation travels at c in a vacuum, whatever its wavelength or frequency.

questions.question: In an electromagnetic wave, the fields oscillate parallel to the direction of travel.
questions.explanation: The wave is transverse: the fields oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel.

questions.question: Which quantities are needed to calculate the speed of a wave? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The wave speed is v = λf, so wavelength and frequency are needed. Amplitude and colour are irrelevant to the speed.

questions.question: Which are true of the E and B fields of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum? Select all that apply.
options: both are perpendicular to the direction of travel
they rise and fall in step
they are parallel to each other
questions.explanation: The fields are mutually perpendicular and both transverse, and they oscillate in phase. They are not parallel to each other.

questions.question: Light has a frequency of 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find its wavelength in nanometres. Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
A wave has a wavelength of 0.10 m and a frequency of 3.0 × 10⁹ Hz. Find its speed in m/s.
A photon is best described as:
options: a discrete packet of electromagnetic energy
a wave that carries no energy
questions.explanation: A photon is the smallest packet of electromagnetic energy, fixed in size by the frequency of the radiation.

questions.question: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its:
questions.explanation: By E = hf, photon energy rises in step with frequency. Longer wavelength means lower frequency and lower energy.

questions.question: Doubling the frequency of light:
options: doubles the energy of each photon
halves the energy of each photon
questions.explanation: E = hf is linear in frequency, so doubling f doubles the photon energy.

questions.question: Which photon carries the most energy?
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet has the highest frequency of the four, so by E = hf it carries the most energy.

questions.question: When light is absorbed, the energy is taken up in whole photons, not in arbitrary amounts.
questions.explanation: Energy is exchanged in discrete quanta. This quantisation is the heart of the quantum picture.

questions.question: The energy of a single photon depends on the intensity of the beam.
questions.explanation: Each photon's energy is set by the frequency alone. Intensity is simply the number of photons arriving per second.

questions.question: Which changes would increase the energy of a photon? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Photon energy depends only on frequency (equivalently, on wavelength through E = hc/λ). Intensity and amplitude do not change it.

questions.question: Which are true of the photon picture? Select all that apply.
options: energy is exchanged in discrete packets
each photon carries a fixed, small amount of energy
photons of all colours carry equal energy
questions.explanation: Energy comes in packets, each of energy E = hf, which is very small. Photons of different colours carry different energies.

questions.question: Find the energy of a photon of frequency 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz, in joules. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
A photon has an energy of 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Find its frequency in hertz. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
Which property is shared by every kind of electromagnetic radiation?
options: it travels at c in a vacuum
it is visible to the eye
it bends in a magnetic field
questions.explanation: Every form of electromagnetic radiation travels at c in a vacuum. Visibility, ionising power and deflection differ between regions.

questions.question: Electromagnetic radiation can cross empty space because:
questions.explanation: The oscillating fields sustain each other, so no material medium is required.

questions.question: The fact that light shows both wave and particle behaviour is called:
questions.explanation: Different experiments reveal different aspects of light; the two pictures are united under wave-particle duality.

questions.question: Which experiment most clearly reveals the particle nature of light?
questions.explanation: The photoelectric effect shows energy being transferred in whole photons, a particle-like behaviour. The others are wave effects.

questions.question: Which experiment most clearly reveals the wave nature of light?
questions.explanation: Interference requires the superposition of waves and cannot be explained by particles travelling independently.

questions.question: Electromagnetic radiation forms a continuous spectrum with no gaps.
questions.explanation: Wavelength and frequency can take any value, so the spectrum is continuous. The named regions simply label bands within it.

questions.question: All electromagnetic radiation is visible to the human eye.
questions.explanation: Only a narrow band, roughly 400–700 nm, is visible. Radio, microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are not.

questions.question: Which are properties of electromagnetic radiation? Select all that apply.
options: travels at c in a vacuum
questions.explanation: It travels at c, needs no medium and is continuous. It is not a mechanical wave, because it needs no matter.

questions.question: Which of the following are wave phenomena? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Interference, diffraction and polarisation are wave effects. The photoelectric effect is evidence of the particle nature.

questions.question: How far does light travel in 2.0 s? Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Give the answer in metres.
A radio wave has a frequency of 1.0 × 10⁶ Hz. Find its wavelength in metres. Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
Which region of the spectrum has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Radio waves lie at the long-wavelength, low-frequency end of the spectrum; gamma rays lie at the other end.

questions.question: Which region has the highest photon energy?
questions.explanation: Photon energy rises with frequency, and gamma rays have the highest frequency of any region.

questions.question: Which ordering runs from shortest to longest wavelength?
options: gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
questions.explanation: The spectrum runs from gamma (shortest) through X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave to radio (longest).

questions.question: As the wavelength decreases across the spectrum, the frequency:
questions.explanation: Because c = λf is fixed, wavelength and frequency move in opposite directions: shorter wavelength means higher frequency.

questions.question: Which radiation is used in medical imaging because its short wavelength lets it pass through soft tissue?
questions.explanation: X-rays have short wavelength and high photon energy, so they penetrate soft tissue but are stopped by bone.

questions.question: Gamma rays have a higher frequency than radio waves.
questions.explanation: Gamma rays sit at the high-frequency end of the spectrum; radio waves at the low-frequency end.

questions.question: Infrared radiation has a shorter wavelength than visible light.
questions.explanation: Infrared is just beyond the red end of the visible band, so its wavelength is longer than visible light.

questions.question: Which regions have a shorter wavelength than visible light? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays all have shorter wavelengths than visible light. Infrared is longer.

questions.question: Which increase as you move from radio waves toward gamma rays? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Frequency and photon energy increase across the spectrum; wavelength decreases; the speed in vacuum stays c.

questions.question: Ultraviolet light has a wavelength of 300 nm. Find its frequency in hertz. Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
The relationship between speed, wavelength and frequency is:
questions.explanation: The wave travels one wavelength per cycle, so speed equals wavelength times frequency.

questions.question: The energy of a photon expressed in terms of its wavelength is:
questions.explanation: Substituting f = c/λ into E = hf gives E = hc/λ, so shorter wavelength means higher energy.

questions.question: If you know a photon's wavelength, you can find its energy using:
questions.explanation: The relation E = hc/λ links energy directly to wavelength through the two constants h and c.

questions.question: Two photons have frequencies in the ratio 1:3. Their energies are in the ratio:
questions.explanation: Energy is proportional to frequency, so the energies share the same ratio as the frequencies: 1:3.

questions.question: A photon of shorter wavelength has more energy than one of longer wavelength.
questions.explanation: Energy is E = hc/λ, so it rises as wavelength falls. Short wavelength means high photon energy.

questions.question: The product of a photon's frequency and its wavelength equals the speed of light.
questions.explanation: That product is exactly c = λf, a restatement of the wave relation.

questions.question: Which of the following relationships are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The first three are correct. E = h/λ is wrong; it is missing the factor c.

questions.question: Find the energy of a photon of wavelength 400 nm, in joules. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
Light has a wavelength of 500 nm. Find its frequency in hertz. Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
